Hematocrit is 35%, and reticulocytes are decreased. Arterial blood gas analysis shows a pH of 7.53 on a FiO₂ of 57%, with an A-a gradient of 375. On physical exam he has eye movements to verbal command (3), is confused (4) and responds to localized pain (5). Decreased sensation is noted bilaterally in the feet extending to the mid-shin. rows.patient_note: A 73-year-old male is admitted to the emergency department following an acute abdominal pain that started suddenly 8 hours ago. He has a known history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, for which he takes insulin daily, and liver cirrhosis. The patient denies any history of cerebrovascular events or ischemic heart disease. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 138/92 mmHg, heart rate is 107 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 35 breaths per minute, and he is afebrile with a temperature of 37.2°C. Auscultation of the chest reveals no rales, S3 gallop, or signs of congestive heart failure. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15, indicating full consciousness. Laboratory results show a creatinine level of 4.58 mg/dL, indicating impaired renal function, and a sodium level of 143.21 mmol/L and a potassium level of 3.68 mmol/L. His fraction of inspired oxygen is 63%. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals a pH of 7.29, a PaO₂ of 78 mm Hg, and an A-a gradient of 331 mm Hg, consistent with significant hypoxemia. Hematocrit is at 41%, and white blood cell count is 15,105 cells/µL. Given his acute presentation, history of diabetes managed with insulin, and laboratory findings, a thorough evaluation including imaging and further laboratory tests is warranted to assess the severity and underlying cause of his symptoms. At present, his management approach does not involve surgical intervention, with close monitoring and reassessment planned.

rows.patient_note: A 57-year-old male presents to the emergency department with generalized weakness and difficulty breathing that started two days ago. His medical history is significant for diabetes mellitus, managed with oral hypoglycemic agents, but no history of cerebrovascular or ischemic heart disease. On examination, his pulse is 73 beats per minute, and he appears slightly dyspneic with a respiratory rate of 27 breaths per minute. Blood pressure is elevated at 132/103 mm Hg. He is afebrile with a temperature of 37.2°C. Laboratory tests reveal a sodium level of 132.39 mmol/L, creatinine of 3.67 mg/dL, potassium of 4.31 mmol/L, and a hematocrit of 32 %. His white blood cell count is 12,476 cells/µL. Arterial blood gas analysis shows a pH of 7.40 and a PaO2 of 57 mm Hg while breathing 32 % oxygen. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15, indicating he is fully alert. The patient has no signs of acute renal failure, though his chronic renal condition and current symptoms suggest a need for careful preoperative management. His history of diabetes and chronic renal failure, combined with current vital signs and laboratory findings, place him at an increased risk for postoperative complications.
